reply:
Still no. You don't need shell access for 777 to matter. A compromised web application running as the nginx user can write there directly. An attacker doesn't need a shell—they need a vulnerability in your code (SQLi leading to file write, XXE, insecure deserialization, dependency exploit). These are common. The upload directory with 777 then becomes the attack surface: plant a PHP shell, execute it via the web server, own the site.

Cost of being wrong: complete site takeover without the attacker needing traditional shell access. Fix it: `chown nginx:nginx upload && chmod 750 upload`.

grade.note: Reiterates original stance with concrete mechanism (compromised app writing as nginx user without shell) and same chown/chmod fix.
